title: Tortoise and hare
summary: Detect a loop in a linked list with two pointers and no extra memory.

cards.title: Runners on a track
cards.body:
Two runners start together. One runs twice as fast. On a straight road, the fast one reaches the end and they never meet again. On a **circular** track, the fast one eventually **laps** the slow one.

Same with pointers: `slow` moves 1 node per step, `fast` moves 2. If they ever point at the same node, the list loops.
The curved arrow under the nodes is the loop back.

cards.title: The code
cards.body: `fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr` is checked **before** `fast->next->next`. Reading through a null pointer is undefined behaviour, usually an instant crash.

cards.title: Why it's clever
cards.body:
The obvious solution remembers every visited node in a set: O(n) extra memory. Floyd's algorithm uses **two pointers**: O(1) memory, still O(n) time.

The trick works on anything that follows "next" links. It's also used to find the cycle length of a **pseudo-random number generator**, which matters when you pick an RNG for a game.

cards.question: The list has no loop and 10 nodes. What stops the loop in `hasCycle`?
cards.explain: fast runs ahead, so it reaches the end first. The while-condition then fails and the function returns false.
